name: Gold Coast Colony
info: The British Crown colony on the Gulf of Guinea, grown from coastal forts taken over in 1821 to the conquest of Asante and the Northern Territories, which became independent as Ghana in 1957.

facts.capital: Cape Coast (Cape Coast Castle), then Christiansborg Castle at Accra after 1874
facts.founder: Sir Charles MacCarthy, governor of Sierra Leone, given authority over the British forts in 1821; Commander Henry Worsley Hill, first governor of the Gold Coast (1843)
facts.predecessor: The nine forts of the African Company of Merchants; the Fante and Ga coastal states; the Asante Empire; the Dutch and Danish Gold Coast

t: The British Crown took over the African Company of Merchants' nine forts in 1821; the Bond of 1844, by which Fante and other chiefs submitted murder and robbery to British jurisdiction, laid the legal basis of the colony proclaimed on 24 July 1874.
British rule was imposed on Asante by war: Kumasi was burnt in 1874, occupied again in 1896 when the asantehene was exiled, and annexed as a colony in 1902 after the War of the Golden Stool.
Cacao trees introduced in 1878 became the colony's mainstay; by the end of the 1940s the Gold Coast exported more than half of the world's cocoa, grown largely by African farmers.
dyk: Kwame Nkrumah won his seat in the Legislative Assembly election of February 1951 while in jail for sedition; the governor, Sir Charles Arden-Clarke, released him and invited him to form a government as 'leader of government business'.
ev: The British Crown dissolves the African Company of Merchants and places its Gold Coast forts under Charles MacCarthy, governor of Sierra Leone.
MacCarthy is killed and most of his force wiped out in a battle with Asante forces; a British, Fante and Accra force defeats an Asante invasion of the coast in 1826.
Commander Henry Worsley Hill negotiates the Bond of 1844 with Fante and other chiefs, who submit murder and robbery to British jurisdiction.
Sir Garnet Wolseley's force occupies and burns Kumasi in January; the coastal protectorate is proclaimed the Gold Coast Colony on 24 July.
A second British expedition occupies Kumasi, makes Asante a protectorate and exiles the asantehene.
After the War of the Golden Stool of 1900 Asante is proclaimed a colony and the Northern Territories a protectorate under the governor of the Gold Coast.
Rioting in Accra and other towns over ex-servicemen's pensions, housing and the foreign hold on the economy; Nkrumah and the UGCC's 'Big Six' are detained.
On 6 March the Colony of the Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana.

sections.foundation:
In the early nineteenth century Asante, the most powerful state of the Akan interior, pressed southward to protect its trade: it invaded the coast in 1807, fought the Ga-Fante War of 1811 and the Ashanti–Akim–Akwapim War of 1814–16, and in 1817 the African Company of Merchants recognised its sovereignty over large areas of the coast. The company held nine trading posts, with Cape Coast Castle as its administrative centre. The Fante and the Ga of the new town of Accra looked to the British for protection, and in 1821 the Crown dissolved the company and gave the forts to Charles MacCarthy, governor of Sierra Leone, with a mandate to impose peace and end the slave trade. In 1824 he was killed and most of his force destroyed by the Asante, who were in turn defeated on the coast in 1826.

Control reverted to the merchants in the late 1820s. From 1830 Captain George Maclean, president of a council of merchants, made peace with Asante in 1831 and held court at Cape Coast; in his thirteen years there were no confrontations and trade reportedly trebled. Crown government returned in 1843 under Commander Henry Worsley Hill, who negotiated the Bond of 1844 with Fante and other chiefs: they were to submit murder and robbery to British jurisdiction, and the document became the legal foundation of British colonisation of the coast. The administration was separated from Sierra Leone in 1850.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Gold Coast had been a major centre of the Atlantic slave trade, and slavery lasted long into British rule. In 1874 Britain declared children born to slaves after 1 January 1875 free and banned debt bondage and pawning, but did not enforce the laws, since the economy depended on slave labour; open slave dealing was tolerated until officials began to act in 1911. The Asante chiefs were assured in 1896 that they could keep their slaves, chattel slavery was formally banned only in 1908, and the ban was not enforced until the 1920s. Gold stayed in African hands until the 1890s, when modern extraction made mining a foreign enterprise: the Ashanti Goldfields Corporation of 1897 gained a concession of about 160 square kilometres, and the European companies and the colonial government took much of the wealth.

Cacao trees, introduced in 1878, gave the farmers of the interior their first cash crop; cocoa became the mainstay of the economy in the 1920s, its production lay largely with Africans, the Cocoa Marketing Board was created in 1947, and by the end of that decade the colony exported more than half of the world's supply. The Sekondi–Tarkwa railway, begun in 1898, reached the chief commercial centres of the south, and by 1937 there were 9,700 kilometres of roads. Export revenue paid for schools and services: Achimota College, the artificial harbour at Takoradi, and in 1948 the University College.
sections.military:
The colony was made by the Anglo-Asante wars. The purchase of the Dutch Gold Coast in 1872 cost Asante its ally at Elmina and its last outlet to the sea, and in 1873 it invaded the coast for the last time. After early successes its army was driven back beyond the Pra River, and Major General Sir Garnet Wolseley rejected a settlement. In January 1874 2,500 British soldiers with large numbers of African auxiliaries invaded Asante and occupied and burnt Kumasi. The treaty that followed made Asante renounce its claims to the southern territories and keep the road to Kumasi open; its power declined as subject territories broke away. In 1896 another expedition occupied Kumasi, made Asante a protectorate, abolished the office of asantehene and exiled its holder. The Asante rose in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900 and were defeated the next year.

The Gold Coast Regiment fought for Britain against German forces in Cameroon and in the long East African campaign of 1914–18, and in the Second World War Gold Coast troops served in Ethiopia and Burma. Their service broadened the veterans' horizons, and they came home in 1945 to inflation, shortages and unemployment, unwilling to accept the humble positions set aside for Africans. Ex-servicemen stood in the forefront of the discontent that broke into rioting and looting in Accra and other towns in early 1948.
sections.governance:
The Gold Coast was four jurisdictions under one governor: the Colony proper on the coast, Asante, the Northern Territories, a protectorate from 1902, and, from 1919, British Togoland. Asante and the north were ruled by resident commissioners and by the governor's proclamations until 1946. From 1850 an Executive Council of European officials and a Legislative Council assisted the governor; after 1900 three chiefs and three other Africans from Accra, Cape Coast and Sekondi joined the Legislative Council, all members were appointed until 1925, and official members always outnumbered the unofficial.

Local rule followed Frederick Lugard's indirect rule, which worked through chiefs; they had ruled by consent and could be destooled by their elders, but under the colonial government they looked to Accra for decisions, and many came to see themselves as an aristocracy rewarded with honours and knighthoods. Provincial councils of chiefs were set up in 1925, the Native Administration Ordinance of 1927 defined their powers, the Native Authorities Ordinance of 1935 joined central and local government, and the Native Treasuries Ordinance of 1939 first allowed local budgets. The Burns constitution of 1946 gave the Legislative Council eighteen elected members and seats for Asante; the constitution of 1951 added an assembly and African ministers, a prime minister followed in 1952, and in 1954 all members were directly elected.
sections.impact:
British rule remade the political map of the region. Asante, which had held sovereignty over much of the coast in 1817, was conquered, its king exiled and its federation dismantled; the Fante and other coastal states, who had sought British protection against it, found the Bond of 1844 set aside in 1874 when their land was annexed without consultation. The borders of present-day Ghana were completed in May 1956, when the people of British Mandated Togoland voted in a United Nations plebiscite to join the Gold Coast. Cocoa, railways, roads and an educational system described as more advanced than any other in West Africa were built on export revenue, and it was through British-style education that a new elite found the means and the will to seek independence.

That elite made the colony the centre of West African nationalism. The Aborigines' Rights Protection Society of the 1890s fought a land bill; in 1920 Joseph E. Casely-Hayford convened the National Congress of British West Africa, the first political solidarity of intellectuals across the British colonies. Kwame Nkrumah, who had attended the Fifth Pan-African Congress in 1945, returned in 1947 and in 1949 founded the Convention People's Party on a mass following of workers, farmers, ex-servicemen, teachers and market women. The Gold Coast's elected majority of 1946 was called a level of political maturity unequalled in colonial Africa.
sections.decline:
The war's end brought inflation, shortages and unemployment. Rioting in Accra and other towns in early 1948 made African power a British priority. The United Gold Coast Convention, founded in August 1947 by J. B. Danquah, Paa Grant and others, demanded self-government 'in the shortest possible time' and the replacement of chiefs on the Legislative Council by educated men; its general secretary Nkrumah, detained in March 1948 with the 'Big Six', broke away in June 1949 to form the Convention People's Party, which asked for 'self-government now'. The Coussey Committee's constitution of 1951 gave the Executive Council a majority of African ministers, and in February 1951 the CPP won two-thirds of the 104 seats with Nkrumah in jail; Sir Charles Arden-Clarke freed him to lead the government.

Nkrumah became prime minister in 1952, and the constitution of 1954 left only defence and foreign policy with the governor. The Asante-based National Liberation Movement and the Northern People's Party demanded a federal constitution and accused the CPP of dictatorial tendencies; when they walked out of talks the governor dissolved the assembly, and the Crown promised independence if two-thirds of the new legislature asked for it. In July 1956 the CPP won 57 per cent of the vote and, with the opposition divided, a two-thirds majority; British Togoland had voted that May to join. On 6 March 1957 the Colony of the Gold Coast became independent as Ghana.

summary: The Gold Coast Colony grew from the British forts taken over in 1821 into a Crown colony that conquered Asante, annexed the Northern Territories and absorbed British Togoland. Its cocoa, gold and schools bred a nationalist movement led by Kwame Nkrumah, and on 6 March 1957 it became independent as Ghana.
references: David Kimble, A Political History of Ghana: The Rise of Gold Coast Nationalism, 1850–1928 (Clarendon Press, 1963)
F. K. Buah, A History of Ghana (Macmillan, 1998)
W. E. F. Ward, A History of Ghana (Allen & Unwin, 1966)
Florence Mabel Bourret, Gold Coast: A Survey of the Gold Coast and British Togoland, 1919–1946 (Stanford University Press, 1949)
W. W. Claridge, A History of the Gold Coast and Ashanti (1915)
Roger S. Gocking, The History of Ghana (2005)

pointDescs.1821: The Crown dissolves the African Company of Merchants and gives its nine Gold Coast forts to Charles MacCarthy, governor of Sierra Leone, to impose peace and end the slave trade.
pointDescs.1824: MacCarthy is killed and most of his force wiped out by the Asante; control of the settlements soon reverts to the merchants.
pointDescs.1831: George Maclean, president of the merchants' council, makes a peace treaty with Asante; in his years to 1843 there are no confrontations and trade reportedly trebles.
pointDescs.1844: Crown government restored, Governor Henry Worsley Hill signs the Bond of 1844 with Fante and other chiefs, the legal foundation of British rule on the coast.
pointDescs.1850: The Gold Coast is separated from Sierra Leone; an Executive Council and a Legislative Council assist the governor, and in 1852 the chiefs at Cape Coast form a legislative assembly.
pointDescs.1874: Wolseley's army burns Kumasi; the coastal protectorate is proclaimed the Gold Coast Colony on 24 July, and the capital moves to Christiansborg at Accra.
pointDescs.1896: A second expedition occupies Kumasi, makes Asante a protectorate and exiles the asantehene; British protection is extended to the north.
pointDescs.1902: Asante, defeated in the War of the Golden Stool, is proclaimed a colony and the Northern Territories a protectorate: the three territories become one unit under the governor.
pointDescs.1919: Frederick Gordon Guggisberg becomes governor and presents a ten-year development programme: transport, water, hospitals, schools, Takoradi harbour and Achimota College; British Togoland is linked to the colony.
pointDescs.1927: The Native Administration Ordinance defines the powers of chiefs and councils; cocoa, the mainstay since the 1920s, is grown largely by African farmers.
pointDescs.1937: The road network reaches 9,700 kilometres, the railway joins the commercial centres of the south, and six African-owned newspapers are published in the decade.
pointDescs.1946: The Burns constitution gives the Legislative Council an elected majority of eighteen and admits Asante; the governor's rule by proclamation over Asante and the north ends.
pointDescs.1948: Riots in Accra and other towns; the Big Six of the UGCC are detained; the University College opens; the Coussey Committee is set up to advise on the path to independence.
pointDescs.1951: The CPP wins two-thirds of the 104 seats in the first Legislative Assembly election; Nkrumah is released from jail to lead the government.
pointDescs.1957: After the CPP's two-thirds majority of July 1956 and British Togoland's vote to join, the Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana on 6 March.

notes: The register's start of 1821 is the Crown's takeover of the forts; the article dates the Gold Coast Colony proper to 24 July 1874 and the single 'dependency' to 1902. The profile treats 1821–1874 as the British forts and protectorate that became the colony.

The article gives Asante's annexation as 1901 in one place and 1902 in two others ('In 1902, the British proclaimed Asante a colony'; 'Asante became a colony in 1901'): 1902 is used, with the War of the Golden Stool fought 1900 and lost 1901.
The founder fact names MacCarthy (1821) and Hill (first governor, 1843); the article names no single founder.

Living-standard remarks (Baten's anthropometric study) are left out as a historiographical judgement rather than an event; the article's phrase 'the colonial period of the 20th century was not particularly bad' is not repeated.
References: Gocking (2005) and Claridge (1915) are listed in the article without a publisher; the Library of Congress Country Study the article incorporates is not listed as a separate work.

Power curve: the peak is set in 1937 (roads, railway, cocoa, newspapers, provincial councils in place) rather than at a dated conquest; 1931 and the Guggisberg years are summarised under 1919 and 1927, dates the article gives.
